rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.1: The rule forbids dynamic heap allocation in contexts where deterministic behavior and resource guarantees are essential. Safety-critical code paths require absolute reliability and the ability to prove system correctness; hard real-time code paths demand timing predictability and bounded resource consumption. Dynamic heap allocation is inherently unpredictable: the time to allocate, the availability of memory, and the behavior of the memory manager are not deterministically bounded. Allowing dynamic allocation in these code paths would undermine the system's ability to meet safety and timing requirements with statistical certainty. Any operation that performs dynamic heap allocation—including `new`, `delete`, `malloc()`, `calloc()`, `realloc()`, and corresponding deallocation calls—when that operation resides in or is called by a code path designated as safety-critical or hard real-time. Also watch for implicit heap allocation through standard library operations that grow memory dynamically (e.g., `std::vector` resize, `std::string` append, container insertions). Allocation in interrupt handlers, task schedulers, and loops invoked from such code paths is especially suspicious; any transitive call into an allocating function is equally subject to the rule. concepts: dynamic heap allocation, new, delete, malloc, calloc, realloc, safety-critical code path, hard real-time code path, non-deterministic timing, memory availability, memory manager, implicit allocation, determinism, resource guarantees
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.2: The rule exists because manual resource management—explicitly freeing memory, file handles, locks, or other system resources—is error-prone and creates unpredictable cleanup behavior. Without RAII, resources leak when exceptions occur, early returns are taken, or cleanup code is accidentally skipped. RAII ties the resource lifecycle (acquisition and release) directly to object construction and destruction, ensuring that every code path exiting an object's scope automatically releases its resources. This guarantees deterministic cleanup and prevents orphaned resources even under exception conditions. Look for: (1) Raw pointers assigned from dynamic allocation (new, malloc) without a wrapper object that owns and guarantees their deletion; (2) Resources acquired in one location and manually released in multiple separate locations or within catch blocks, creating paths where release can be bypassed; (3) Exception-unsafe patterns where a resource is acquired and cleanup code appears later in the same function, allowing exceptions between acquisition and cleanup to leave the resource dangling; (4) Multiple function exit points (return statements, exception throws, break/continue in loops) where the same dynamically allocated resource must be manually freed at each one; (5) System resource acquisition (file open, mutex lock, dynamic memory) not immediately wrapped in an object constructor whose destructor guarantees release. concepts: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, Object lifetime, Constructor/destructor pairing, Automatic resource release, Exception safety, Ownership semantics, Deterministic cleanup, Resource leak prevention, Manual resource management risks, Tied acquisition and release
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.3: When dynamically allocated memory is owned through raw pointers, the programmer assumes manual responsibility for invoking delete at the correct point in the control-flow path and under all exception scenarios. This manual lifetime management is error-prone: delete may be omitted (memory leak), invoked prematurely (dangling pointer), called twice (double-deletion), or forgotten in exception handlers or branches. Smart pointers encode ownership semantics into the type system and apply RAII principles to guarantee deterministic, automatic deallocation when the owning pointer is destroyed. For safety-critical systems, automating resource cleanup through smart pointers eliminates entire categories of memory-safety errors and ensures predictable lifetime management across all code paths. Raw pointers assigned to newly allocated objects via new; explicit delete statements on raw pointers in application code; raw pointer class members intended to manage the lifetime of dynamically allocated objects; functions that return raw pointers to newly allocated memory without clear ownership transfer documentation; multiple return paths or exception handlers where delete is scattered or potentially missed; ownership passing between raw pointers without enforcement. concepts: dynamically allocated memory, owned, ownership, smart pointers, raw pointers, manual lifetime management, automatic deallocation, RAII, memory leak, dangling pointer, double-deletion, exception safety, deterministic cleanup
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.4: The rule requires that ownership of dynamically allocated resources be explicit and unambiguous to prevent resource leaks, double-deletion, and use-after-free errors in safety-critical systems. When code allocates memory on the heap, it must clearly designate which entity—a caller, callee, owning container, or resource wrapper—holds responsibility for deallocation. If ownership is implicit or ambiguous, resources may be abandoned (leaking memory), freed multiple times, or accessed after deallocation. Uncontrolled resource lifecycle faults undermine system reliability and can trigger undefined behavior. Code patterns where dynamically allocated resources lack explicit ownership signals include: functions returning raw pointers with no indication whether the caller or callee owns the result; pointer parameters passed into functions without documented responsibility transfer; raw pointers stored in containers or passed between functions with no clear ownership semantics; allocations performed in one scope and deallocations scattered across multiple call sites; absence of a consistent resource-management convention (such as RAII, smart pointers, or ownership contracts); and raw new/delete expressions unaccompanied by code structure, comments, or function contracts that clarify when and by whom the resource will be freed. concepts: resource ownership, dynamically allocated memory, explicit responsibility, unambiguous deallocation, ownership transfer, raw pointers, memory management, resource lifecycle, caller versus callee responsibility, heap allocation, ownership semantics
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.5: The rule forbids dereferencing a pointer when the object that pointer refers to has ended its lifetime. This prohibition exists because dereferencing such a pointer—accessing memory that is no longer allocated to that object—is undefined behavior. By enforcing this constraint, the rule preserves memory safety and prevents crashes, corruption, or exploitation that arises from accessing memory that is no longer valid or owned by the program. Typical code shapes that trigger this rule involve dereferencing a pointer to: (a) a local object after the block or function scope in which that object was declared has ended; (b) an object that has been freed or deleted, where the pointer persists and is later dereferenced; (c) a temporary object after its lifetime has expired; (d) an object in a container that has been cleared or deallocated, invalidating all pointers into it; (e) an object whose lifetime was terminated by exception unwinding, context exit, or resource cleanup. concepts: pointer, dereference, object lifetime, dangling pointer, use-after-free, memory safety, undefined behavior, pointer validity
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.6: Raw pointer arithmetic operates without inherent bounds enforcement, allowing accidental or malicious access beyond intended memory regions. By prohibiting direct arithmetic and mandating bounded abstractions, the rule ensures that all pointer-based memory access is mediated through mechanisms that verify or enforce logical bounds. This prevents undefined behavior arising from out-of-bounds traversal, buffer overflows, and memory corruption in safety-critical contexts. Direct increment/decrement of raw pointers (ptr++, ptr--); arithmetic expressions combining pointers and integers (ptr + offset, ptr - count); loops that step pointers without bounds validation; pointer casts followed by arithmetic; sequential pointer dereferences where the validity of the target address depends on unchecked calculations. concepts: raw pointer arithmetic, bounded abstractions, memory bounds enforcement, pointer traversal safety, out-of-bounds prevention, undefined behavior, memory safety invariants
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.7: This rule exists to prevent undefined behavior and heap corruption that arises from mismatched allocation and deallocation forms in C++. When a resource is allocated with `new`, it must be released with `delete` (not `delete[]`, `free()`, or other release mechanisms). When allocated with `new[]`, it must be released with `delete[]`. Mismatches cause the memory allocator to apply incorrect cleanup logic to heap metadata, corrupting the heap state and leading to crashes, data corruption, or exploitable vulnerabilities. In safety-critical code, such undefined behavior is unacceptable because it violates the predictability and auditability requirements of the system. Code patterns that misuse deallocation operators: using `delete` on pointers allocated via `new[]` (especially string or buffer arrays); using `delete[]` on single objects allocated via `new`; mixing C-style allocation (`malloc`, `calloc`) with C++ deallocation operators (`delete`, `delete[]`); pointer parameters or return values where the allocation form is unclear or undocumented; raw pointers passed between functions where the original allocator is not traceable; template code or polymorphic classes where the concrete allocation type is hidden; conditional branches that allocate the same variable with different forms; and long object lifetimes where allocation and deallocation are separated by significant code, making the match hard to verify. concepts: new/delete pairing, new[]/delete[] pairing, allocation form matching, deallocation operator selection, undefined behavior, heap corruption, memory management safety, resource lifecycle, pointer ownership, single-object vs. array semantics
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.8: The C++ runtime distinguishes between scalar memory allocation (new) and array allocation (new[]). Array allocations store metadata (such as element count) to enable proper construction and destruction of all elements. Using scalar delete on array-allocated memory causes the destructor to execute only on the first element, corrupts the stored metadata, and leads to resource leaks and undefined behavior. This rule enforces a strict invariant: the deallocation form must match the allocation form. Raw pointers assigned from new[] but subsequently deleted with scalar delete; patterns where new[] allocations are passed through function boundaries or stored in containers without preserving knowledge of the allocation form; code that deletes pointer variables without explicit verification of whether they were allocated with new or new[]. concepts: array new[], array delete[], scalar delete, allocation form matching, element destruction, metadata corruption, heap undefined behavior, destructor invocation sequence, memory safety
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.9: A dynamically allocated resource (memory obtained via new, new[], malloc, or similar allocators) must transition to a released state exactly once. Invoking a deallocator (delete, delete[], free, release) on the same pointer a second time is undefined behavior — the heap manager's internal state is corrupted because the memory has already been marked as free and may have been reallocated to satisfy another request. The guideline forbids this single most dangerous form of memory management error, which leads to heap corruption, process termination, or silent security violations. Code patterns that invoke a deallocator on a pointer that has already been released in the same execution path: explicit sequential deletes on the same variable; deletion in both a normal code path and an exception handler operating on the same pointer; deallocation via one ownership interface (e.g., function A calls delete) followed by deallocation via another (e.g., function B also calls delete on a pointer it received); absence of null assignment after the first deallocator call (so a second invocation is not guarded); pointer aliasing where the same heap block is tracked by multiple variables and cleaned up multiple times; and RAII or smart-pointer violations where destructor cleanup overlaps with explicit deallocation. concepts: double free, pointer deallocator, resource lifecycle, memory ownership, heap state, undefined behavior, single release guarantee, pointer reuse, exception safety
rules.MISRA-CPP-2023-Rule-22.10: Weak pointers hold non-owning references to objects whose lifetime is managed by owning references elsewhere (e.g., shared pointers). The object may be deallocated while weak pointers to it remain, rendering them invalid and dangling. Locking a weak pointer via lock() produces either a valid owning pointer if the object is still alive, or a null owning pointer if the object has been destroyed. Null-checking this result confirms the object exists before use. This lock-then-null-check sequence is a mandatory safety gate before any dereference, member access, or method call on the pointed-to object. Violation risks use-after-free: dereferencing a pointer to memory that no longer contains the intended live object. Code shapes include: dereferencing or accessing members of a weak pointer directly without calling lock() first (e.g., weak_ptr->member, weak_ptr.operator->(), (*weak_ptr).field), using weak_ptr.get() to extract a raw pointer and dereferencing it without the preceding lock-and-null-check, calling methods or accessing properties on the weak pointer itself as though it held ownership, using a weak pointer in a conditional, loop, or expression context without first confirming via lock() and null-check that the object remains valid, constructing an owning pointer from a weak pointer without the lock-and-check sequence, and calling lock() but then neglecting to test the returned pointer for null before any use. concepts: weak pointer, lock, owning pointer, non-owning reference, null check, object lifetime, dangling reference, use-after-free, validity, deallocation
